title: Whose growth chart? Models default to American norms
line: counterfactual nationality experiment on growth-chart choice
question: A healthy Korean toddler or Indian adolescent plotted on a US chart can look abnormal. When a language model assesses a child's growth, does it pick the right national reference, or judge every child against American norms?
skills: growth reference standards (CDC, WHO, national charts)
data: 37 chart-choice prompts, the same child with the population descriptor swapped
CDC 2000 and WHO 2006 references, national charts for comparison
found: without a stated population, 96% of responses judged the child against a US chart (89 of 98).
naming the population helps unevenly: told the child is Korean, 57% still used a US chart; for South-Asian children, 17.5% picked the correct national chart.
models reason fluently about growth but rarely say that the reference population matters at all.
calls: the descriptor is one word (Korean, South Asian, Indian, Dutch) with nothing else changed, so any shift comes from the label and not from extra clinical detail.
scored on whether the model names the reference it used, not only on the final call. a correct call against the wrong chart is still a reference failure.
broke: responses were scored by an LLM judge; a human audit of the judge's calls is still to do.
the Dutch and South-Asian cases use proxy references until exact LMS tables are substituted.
